opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think people sometimes talk about MCTS as if it's this magic box: you wrap it around a policy and out comes a strictly better policy. In practice it's more subtle than that.

What MCTS actually does is spend extra compute at decision time to look ahead, using the policy network as a prior over which moves to explore and the value network to estimate how good the leaf positions are. Then it aggregates those estimates back up the tree. If your value estimates were perfect and you could search exhaustively, you'd get an improvement. But neither of those is true. You're searching a tiny fraction of the tree, and the leaf evaluations are themselves just neural network guesses.

So the search is only as good as the signals it's built on. If the value network is systematically wrong about some class of positions, search can confidently amplify that error. It might steer toward lines the value net loves that are actually losing. There's no theorem saying that a few hundred simulations with an approximate value function beat the raw policy's intuition. Empirically it usually helps, often a lot, which is why it worked so well in AlphaGo and AlphaZero. But that's an empirical regularity, not a guarantee.

There's also a lot of design freedom baked in: the exploration constant, how you trade off prior versus visit counts, how many simulations you run, temperature when you pick the final move. Those are knobs people tuned until it worked. That's a hallmark of a heuristic. It's a well-engineered procedure that tends to produce a better policy target, and that's exactly what you want for the self-improvement loop. You distill the search policy back into the network and repeat. But the reason the loop works is that, on average, search plus a decent value function is a bit sharper than the raw prior. It isn't because search is provably correct.

And I think that framing matters when people try to port the idea to other domains like language models or robotics. Your value function there is often much noisier, and the environment may be stochastic or hard to simulate. So the "search makes things better" assumption can break down. You have to earn it with a good enough model and a good enough value estimate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing people forget about AlphaGo and AlphaZero is that MCTS isn't magic. It's a search procedure that's bootstrapped off the policy network and the value network, and those are learned functions. The search is only as good as the priors it's using to expand nodes and the value estimates it's using to back up. If the value network is wrong about some board position, search doesn't fix that for free. It can actually amplify the error, because now you're spending compute confidently exploring a line that the value head thinks is great and it isn't.

So when you look at it from a learning perspective, the claim "search is a policy improvement operator" is really a claim about expectation. On average, across a lot of positions, rolling out with the value function and picking the action with the best visit count gives you a slightly better move distribution than the raw policy. That's the amortization loop that makes AlphaZero work. But it's not a guarantee at the level of any individual state. There are plenty of positions where the raw network's intuition is better than what you get after a budget of simulations, especially when the budget is small or the tree is very wide.

And then there's the structural stuff. MCTS assumes a discrete action space, a simulator you can step forward perfectly, usually deterministic dynamics or something close to it. The moment you go to robotics, where I spend most of my time, none of that holds. You don't have a perfect world model, actions are continuous, and the thing you're really uncertain about is the dynamics, not the opponent. So search in that setting is a heuristic in an even stronger sense. You're searching through a model that's itself a learned approximation, and the value of the search depends entirely on how good that model is in the regions you're exploring.

I'd put it this way: the policy network is the thing that actually generalizes. Search is a way to spend test-time compute to patch up where the policy is locally wrong. That's useful, and it's probably the right way to think about a lot of what's happening with reasoning models now too. But it's a trick that works because of properties of the problem, not a theorem that says more search always beats the network. If it were a free improvement we wouldn't need to distill it back into the policy. The fact that we do tells you the network is where the knowledge lives.

astra-6.text:
Because search is only as good as what’s guiding it. If you could search all the way to the end of the game and evaluate every outcome exactly, then you’d have a guarantee. But that’s not what we’re doing. We have a finite compute budget, we use the policy to decide which branches to explore, and we use a learned value function to evaluate positions where we stop.

So you can take an action that the policy initially liked, look ahead, and conclude that some other action is better—but that conclusion might just reflect an error in your value function. Search can amplify those errors. And if the policy assigns very little probability to a good move, you might not spend enough compute exploring it in the first place.

That doesn’t mean search isn’t useful. It can be extremely useful. It means that calling it a policy improvement operator is an empirical claim in this setting, rather than a guarantee that every additional bit of search makes the policy better.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, search is only as good as the thing you’re using to evaluate the search. If you could roll out every possible continuation and evaluate the actual outcome, then you’d have a much stronger guarantee. But in practice, you have a finite compute budget, you’re sampling a tiny fraction of the tree, and you’re often using a learned value function to decide which branches look promising.

That value function can be wrong. And search can amplify that error: you spend more compute finding a continuation that your evaluator thinks is great, but that isn’t actually great. You’re optimizing against the evaluator’s mistakes.

The policy network also contains information that isn’t necessarily captured by your search procedure. So overriding its judgment with a limited search doesn’t automatically improve the decision. It often does empirically, especially in settings where you have reliable feedback, but that’s an empirical result, not a general guarantee that more search makes the policy better.
